extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of early modern philosophy (Locke)
extracted.subtask_description: Close reading of John Locke's account of ideas of substance, spirit, collective ideas, and relation from An Essay Concerning Human Understanding (Chapters XXIII–XXV). Emphasizes how complex ideas are built from simple ideas and how relations are formed by comparison.

rubrics_metrics.name: Idea of body (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Our idea of BODY, as I think, is AN EXTENDED SOLID SUBSTANCE, CAPABLE OF COMMUNICATING MOTION BY IMPULSE.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is presented as the mind’s complex idea of body; Locke contrasts it directly with the idea of soul and uses it as the basis for further discussion of cohesion, extension, and impulse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Idea of soul (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Our idea of SOUL, AS AN IMMATERIAL SPIRIT, is of A SUBSTANCE THAT THINKS, AND HAS A POWER OF EXCITING MOTION IN BODY, BY WILLING, OR THOUGHT.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke frames this as the complex idea of soul and compares its obscurities to those of body; used to argue that notion of an immaterial spirit is no more problematic than that of extended matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complex ideas of substances built from simple ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: All our ideas of the several SORTS of substances are nothing but collections of simple ideas: with a supposition of SOMETHING to which they belong, and in which they subsist; though of this supposed something we have no clear distinct idea at all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeated claim: complex (e.g., man, gold, God) ideas are aggregates of simple ideas 'received from sensation or reflection'; any attempt to go beyond those simple ideas leads to obscurity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple ideas from sensation or reflection are the limits of thought
rubrics_metrics.description: The simple ideas that make up complex ideas are no other but such as we have received from sensation or reflection; beyond these ideas the mind cannot reach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke uses this as a methodological standard: when analyzing concepts (even God or spirits), one must trace their constituents to sensation or reflection; claims about natures beyond those constituents are speculative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideas of relations arise from comparing two things
rubrics_metrics.description: Relation is the considering of one thing with another which is extrinsical to it; when the mind so considers one thing, that it does as it were bring it to, and set it by another...this is, as the words import, RELATION and RESPECT.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical test: to identify a relation, show the mind is led beyond the denominated subject to another thing; relative terms serve as marks to lead thoughts beyond the primary subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative terms lead the mind beyond the subject denominated
rubrics_metrics.description: All words that necessarily lead the mind to any other ideas than are supposed really to exist in that thing to which the words are applied are relative words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'father', 'brother', 'king', 'husband', 'blacker' are relative because they imply something external; contrast with absolute terms like 'man', 'black', 'angry' which do not by themselves imply another distinct thing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation requires two things (binary nature)
rubrics_metrics.description: There can be no relation but betwixt two things considered as two things. There must always be in relation two ideas or things, either in themselves really separate, or considered as distinct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use as criterion: any alleged relation must specify the two relata; relations do not exist in isolation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collective ideas are single ideas formed by composition
rubrics_metrics.description: A collective idea is one Idea...because such ideas are made up of many particular substances considered together, as united into one idea, and which so joined; are looked on as one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: army, swarm, city, fleet, universe—the mind composes multiple distinct particulars into one unified idea for contemplation and discourse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artificial composite things count as collective ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Amongst such kind of collective ideas are to be counted most part of artificial things, at least such of them as are made up of distinct substances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical implication: when analyzing artifacts composed of diverse parts, treat them as collective ideas formed by mental composition rather than irreducible simple substances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Some apparently absolute terms conceal relations
rubrics_metrics.description: Another sort of relative terms...which under the form and appearance of signifying something absolute in the subject, do conceal a tacit, though less observable, relation. Such are the seemingly positive terms of OLD, GREAT, IMPERFECT, &c.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analytic caution: probe supposed absolute descriptors for hidden comparatives or relational bases (e.g., 'old' presupposes aging relative to something).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideas of relation often clearer than ideas of substances
rubrics_metrics.description: The ideas which relative words stand for are often clearer and more distinct than of those substances to which they do belong. THE IDEAS, THEN, OF RELATIONS, ARE CAPABLE AT LEAST OF BEING MORE PERFECT AND DISTINCT IN OUR MINDS THAN THOSE OF SUBSTANCES.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this as an interpretive heuristic: one can often attain a precise notion of a relation (e.g., paternity) without having a fully clear idea of the underlying substance (e.g., humanity).

rubrics_metrics.name: All relations terminate in simple ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Though there be a great number of considerations wherein things may be compared one with another...yet they all terminate in, and are concerned about those simple ideas, either of sensation or reflection, which I think to be the whole materials of all our knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argumentative standard: when accounting for even remote relations, trace them back to simple ideas; this undergirds Locke’s epistemological reductionism.

rubrics_metrics.name: No idea of spirits or God beyond simple ideas except infinity
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no idea we attribute to God, bating infinity, which is not also a part of our complex idea of other spirits...we can attribute to spirits no other but what we receive from reflection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methodological note: in forming concepts of spirits or God, we enlarge simple reflective ideas (existence, knowledge, power) by extension (e.g., infinity); otherwise our ideas are composed from the same mental materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communication of motion by impulse and by thought equally unintelligible
rubrics_metrics.description: These ideas, the one of body, the other of our minds, every day’s experience clearly furnishes us with: but if here again we inquire how this is done, we are equally in the dark...we have clear evidence of motion produced both by impulse and by thought; but the manner how, hardly comes within our comprehension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Epistemic humility: accept experiential evidence for both bodily and mental causation while recognizing both mechanisms elude complete understanding; do not privilege the intelligibility of one over the other without argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalence of difficulty between conceiving spirit and conceiving body
rubrics_metrics.description: This notion of immaterial spirit may have some difficulties in it not easily to be explained; we have therefore no more reason to deny or doubt the existence of such spirits, than we have to deny or doubt the existence of body...the notion of body is cumbered with some difficulties very hard, and perhaps impossible to be explained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critical standard: avoid dismissing immaterial substances merely because they seem obscure—Locke argues that material substances are equally problematic on closer inspection.
